rationale: The plant uses a hazardous chemical, so it must maintain its written hazard communication program and hazardous-chemical list, have an accessible SDS, and ensure workplace containers are labeled, tagged, or marked. Because this is a new chemical hazard on which the employees have not previously been trained, effective hazard communication information and training is required when introduced into their work area. Training must cover the required hazard, protective-measure, labeling-system, SDS, and program-information topics. The immediate-use portable-container labeling exception is not selected because the facts do not establish that each transferred container is intended only for the immediate use of the employee performing the transfer.

predicted_citations: Each employee presently involved in operating a process, and each employee before being involved in operating a newly assigned process, shall be trained in an overview of the process and in the operating procedures as specified in paragraph (f) of this section.

The employer shall ascertain that each employee involved in operating a process has received and understood the training required by this paragraph. The employer shall prepare a record which contains the identity of the employee, the date of training, and the means used to verify that the employee understood the training.

Employers shall provide employees with effective information and training on hazardous chemicals in their work area at the time of their initial assignment, and whenever a new chemical hazard the employees have not previously been trained about is introduced into their work area.

Employees shall be informed of: The requirements of this section; Any operations in their work area where hazardous chemicals are present; and, The location and availability of the written hazard communication program.

Employee training shall include at least:
(i) Methods and observations that may be used to detect the presence or release of a hazardous chemical in the work area (such as monitoring conducted by the employer, continuous monitoring devices, visual appearance or odor of hazardous chemicals when being released, etc.)
(ii) The physical, health, simple asphyxiation, combustible dust, and pyrophoric gas hazards, as well as hazards not otherwise classified, of the chemicals in the work area
(iii) The measures employees can take to protect themselves from these hazards, including specific procedures the employer has implemented to protect employees from exposure to hazardous chemicals, such as appropriate work practices, emergency procedures, and personal protective equipment to be used
(iv) The details of the hazard communication program developed by the employer, including an explanation of the labels received on shipped containers and the workplace labeling system used by their employer; the safety data sheet, including the order of information and how employees can obtain and use the appropriate hazard information
rationale: The technician is an employee newly assigned to operate a process covered by §1910.119. Before operating that newly assigned process next week, the employee must receive PSM training covering a process overview and applicable operating procedures. The employer must ascertain and document that the employee received and understood the training, including identity, training date, and verification method. Because the work area involves highly hazardous chemicals, initial-assignment hazard communication information and training is also triggered, including the specified hazard, protective-measure, program, label, and safety-data-sheet topics.

Federal OSHA PSM applies, and the stated equipment and technology modification is not a replacement in kind and changes process safety information. The employer must manage the change through written MOC procedures, address the specified MOC considerations, update affected process safety information and operating procedures, and inform and train affected operating, maintenance, and contract employees before startup. Because the modification is significant enough to require a change in process safety information, a pre-startup safety review is required. Before highly hazardous chemicals are introduced, that review must confirm equipment conforms to design specifications, adequate safety/operating/maintenance/emergency procedures are in place, MOC has been met for the modified facility, and operator training is complete. Equipment compliance with recognized and generally accepted good engineering practices and records verifying employee training are also required.

This near miss occurred at a PSM-covered process and could reasonably have resulted in a catastrophic toxic release. The employer must investigate it, initiate the investigation as promptly as possible and no later than 48 hours after the incident (36 hours remain based on the supplied timing), document resolution and corrective actions for findings and recommendations, review the report with affected personnel including applicable contract employees, and retain the investigation report for five years. The absence of an injury does not eliminate the PSM incident-investigation obligation.

Because the establishment is required to keep Part 1904 records and had 300 employees, it must review and correct the OSHA 300 Log, create and certify the annual summary, post it conspicuously no later than February 1 through April 30, electronically submit Form 300A information, and retain the required records for five years.

The described equipment is within the supplied lockout/tagout context because unexpected energization or stored energy could cause injury during servicing. As the anniversary of the last machine-specific energy-control-procedure review approaches, the employer must conduct the periodic inspection at least annually to ensure the procedure and standard requirements are being followed.

The stated activity is covered servicing, and the stated hazards are unexpected startup and release of stored pneumatic energy capable of causing injury. The employer must maintain an energy-control program; develop, document, and use machine-specific hazardous-energy-control procedures; provide isolating hardware and employee training; inspect the procedure at least annually; isolate all required energy sources; and relieve, disconnect, restrain, or otherwise render stored pneumatic energy safe after lockout/tagout devices are applied.

Because the contractor is being selected to work in a covered PSM process area and will face known fire, explosion, and toxic-release hazards, the host employer must evaluate the contract employer's safety performance and programs; communicate known hazards and applicable emergency-action-plan provisions; and implement safe work practices governing contractor entrance, presence, and exit. The contract employer must train and instruct its employees, document their receipt and understanding of required training, ensure compliance with facility safety rules, and communicate unique or discovered contractor-work hazards. The host also must maintain a contractor injury-and-illness log related to work in process areas.

The requester is a former employee seeking the OSHA 301 Incident Report describing that former employee's own injury, and the employer maintains the requested report. The cited provision expressly requires providing that report by the end of the next business day.

Because the requester is an authorized employee representative for employees at the establishment under a collective bargaining agreement, the employer must provide the requested OSHA 301 Incident Report case information within 7 calendar days. The copy must include only the section titled "Tell us about the case," with all other information removed.

The establishment is recordkeeping-covered, and the case is stated to be a new, work-related fatality. Death satisfies the general recording criteria. The employer must report the fatality to OSHA within 8 hours, enter the recordable case on the OSHA 300 Log and OSHA 301 Incident Report within 7 calendar days of receiving information of the case, and retain the specified records for 5 years following the end of the covered calendar year.

The work-related incident resulted in both an employee amputation and in-patient hospitalization. Report the event to OSHA within 24 hours. Because the case is stipulated to be recordable and the employer learned of it today, enter it on the OSHA 300 Log and complete the OSHA 301 Incident Report within seven calendar days of receiving that information. Retain the OSHA 300 Log, OSHA 301 Incident Report, annual summary, and any privacy case list for five years after the end of the calendar year covered.

The new-employee orientation supports the requirement to inform each employee of the employer's work-related injury and illness reporting procedure. The employer must maintain a reporting procedure that does not deter or discourage accurate reporting, and must not discharge or otherwise discriminate against an employee for reporting a work-related injury or illness. A supervisor's threat of discipline after such a report is inconsistent with these reporting-protection requirements.

Because the covered process is undergoing its required three-year PSM compliance audit and deficiencies were identified, the employer must promptly determine and document an appropriate response to every audit finding and document correction of deficiencies. The employer must retain the two most recent compliance-audit reports.

The scheduled inspection of covered-process equipment triggers the PSM mechanical-integrity inspection and documentation requirement. Because the vessel is outside acceptable limits, it must be corrected before further use, unless it can be corrected safely and timely while necessary means assure safe operation. Determining whether continued operation is safely assured requires qualified engineering and process-safety judgment.
missing_information_or_escalation_reason: A qualified determination is needed regarding the deficiency, whether the vessel will be used before correction, the applicable process-safety-information limits, and what necessary measures—if any—would assure safe operation pending correction.

rationale: Federal OSHA Hazard Communication applies, the employer uses the hazardous chemical in the employee's work area, and the employee could not immediately access its SDS during the night shift. The employer must have an SDS in the workplace for each hazardous chemical used and must ensure that required SDS copies are readily accessible during each work shift to employees in their work areas. The stated inability to immediately access the SDS directly implicates the accessibility requirement.

The portable container is filled from a labeled container, intended only for the immediate use of the employee performing the transfer, and remains under that employee's control rather than being stored. Therefore, the employer is not required to label the portable container under the stated exception.

The applicable rule requires that each lockout or tagout device be removed by the employee who applied it. The supplied excerpt does not state any exception or the conditions and authorization required for an employer-directed removal when that employee is absent. Because management proposes removal by another employee, determining whether and how that may occur requires qualified safety/legal review of the employer's energy-control procedure and the relevant complete regulatory provisions.
missing_information_or_escalation_reason: Escalate before removal. The supplied context lacks the employer’s documented energy-control procedure for absent-employee lock removal, including its authorization, verification, notification, and safe-removal requirements; it also lacks facts confirming the equipment’s energy-isolated and stored-energy-safe condition.

rationale: Because one employer's hazardous chemicals may expose employees of another employer at the shared worksite, the employer that produces, uses, or stores those chemicals must ensure its written hazard communication program states the methods used to provide the other on-site employer access to the safety data sheet for each hazardous chemical.

The proposed component has a different material specification and operating limit, while engineering and operations disagree whether it is technically equivalent. The record therefore does not support conclusively treating it as a replacement in kind, which is the exception to the PSM management-of-change requirement. A qualified engineering/process-safety determination is needed. If it is a covered change, written MOC procedures must address the technical basis, safety and health impact, operating-procedure modifications, timing, and authorization before the change; affected employees must be informed and trained before startup. Equipment compliance with recognized and generally accepted good engineering practices must be documented, and process safety information must be updated if the change affects it.
missing_information_or_escalation_reason: Escalate to qualified process-safety and engineering personnel to determine replacement-in-kind status using the approved design/process-safety-information specifications, applicable engineering standards, component service conditions, and the effect of the changed material and operating limit on process hazards and equipment integrity. Confirm whether the proposed installation changes process safety information; if so, update it under §1910.119(l)(4) and complete the applicable MOC actions before startup.

rationale: A 24-hour OSHA report is required only when an employee's in-patient hospitalization results from a work-related incident. The supplied facts establish neither work-relatedness nor that the hospital admission was in-patient treatment. The weekend timing alone does not resolve either predicate.
missing_information_or_escalation_reason: Determine whether the illness resulted from a work-related incident and whether the employee was formally admitted for in-patient hospitalization.

rationale: New hazard training is required whenever a new chemical hazard that employees have not previously been trained about is introduced into their work area. Ordering a product alone does not establish that it is hazardous, that it will be introduced into employees' work area, or that it presents an untrained hazard.
missing_information_or_escalation_reason: Determine from the product's hazard information (such as its safety data sheet) whether it is a hazardous chemical and will introduce a chemical hazard in the employees' work area that they have not previously been trained about; confirm the employees' existing hazard-training coverage.

rationale: Outside servicing personnel must exchange their respective lockout/tagout procedures with the on-site employer only when they will perform activities covered by the lockout/tagout standard. Coverage for maintenance depends on whether unexpected energization, startup, or release of stored energy could occur and cause injury. That material predicate is not supplied.
missing_information_or_escalation_reason: Determine for the planned maintenance whether the equipment has energy sources or stored/residual energy and whether unexpected energization, startup, or energy release could cause injury. If yes, the work is covered and the site and vendor must inform each other of their respective lockout/tagout procedures.

rationale: The establishment's 75 employees place it within the 20-249 employee range specified by §1904.41(a)(1)(i), and it keeps Part 1904 records. However, electronic submission of Form 300A information is required for that size range only if the establishment is classified in an industry listed in appendix A to subpart E. The industry classification is not supplied.
missing_information_or_escalation_reason: Provide the establishment's industry classification and whether that classification is listed in appendix A to subpart E of Part 1904.
